lessonTitle: Transcription and RNA Processing: RNA Polymerase II, Capping, Splicing, Polyadenylation and Alternative Splicing

blocks.text: A single base change at the very edge of an intron can leave the genetic message intact but stop the cell from cutting it out correctly, causing an inherited anaemia. In a typical human gene, the RNA copy is cut down to a fraction of its original length before it ever leaves the nucleus. Making that copy and editing it are the two halves of this unit.

blocks.markdown: **From DNA to RNA.** In **transcription**, the information in a gene is copied into RNA. The enzyme **RNA polymerase** reads the **template (antisense) strand** of DNA in the 3' to 5' direction and synthesises RNA in the 5' to 3' direction, using ribonucleoside triphosphates, with uracil (U) replacing thymine, and, unlike DNA polymerase, it needs no primer. The RNA therefore has the same sequence as the **coding (sense) strand** (with U in place of T). In human cells three nuclear polymerases transcribe different genes: **RNA polymerase I** (most ribosomal RNA), **RNA polymerase II** (all protein-coding genes, giving pre-mRNA, as well as many non-coding RNAs) and **RNA polymerase III** (tRNA, 5S rRNA and other small RNAs). This lesson focuses on polymerase II.

blocks.title: Promoter and general transcription factors
blocks.text: A promoter is a DNA sequence near the start of a gene where RNA polymerase binds. Many eukaryotic promoters contain a TATA box about 25-30 base pairs upstream of the transcription start. RNA polymerase II cannot bind DNA on its own; it requires general transcription factors (TFIID, which includes the TATA-binding protein, TFIIB, TFIIF, TFIIE and TFIIH) to assemble the preinitiation complex.

blocks.markdown: **The stages of transcription by RNA polymerase II.** (1) **Initiation:** TFIID (via the TATA-binding protein) binds the TATA box and bends the DNA; the other general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II assemble to form the **preinitiation complex**. The helicase activity of TFIIH unwinds about 10-15 base pairs of DNA (the open complex) and its kinase phosphorylates the **C-terminal domain (CTD)** of the polymerase, releasing it from the promoter. Gene-specific activators and enhancers (covered in the next unit) increase the rate of initiation. (2) **Elongation:** the polymerase moves along the template, unwinding DNA ahead and rewinding behind it, adding ribonucleotides to the 3' end of the growing RNA; the phosphorylated CTD acts as a platform to recruit the capping, splicing and polyadenylation machinery. (3) **Termination:** the polymerase transcribes past a polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA); the RNA is cleaved about 10-30 nucleotides downstream, and the polymerase is released after further transcription.

blocks.title: Writing the RNA from a template
blocks.prompt: The template (antisense) strand of a gene segment reads 3'-TACCGATTG-5'. Write the mRNA sequence, state its polarity, and give the sequence of the coding strand.

steps.text: RNA is synthesised 5' to 3' using the template strand read 3' to 5'. Pair each template base with its complementary RNA base: T pairs with A, A with U, C with G, G with C. Template 3'-T A C C G A T T G-5' gives:
The coding strand is complementary to the template and so has the same sequence as the RNA but with T in place of U: 5'-ATGGCTAAC-3'.

blocks.markdown: **RNA processing.** The primary transcript, **pre-mRNA** or heterogeneous nuclear RNA, is not a functional mRNA. It is modified in the nucleus, mostly while it is still being made. (1) **5' capping:** a 7-methylguanosine is added to the 5' end by an unusual 5'-5' triphosphate linkage. The cap protects the mRNA from 5' exonucleases, helps export from the nucleus and is recognised by initiation factors in translation. (2) **Splicing:** non-coding **introns** are removed and **exons** are joined by the **spliceosome**, a complex of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) and proteins. Introns usually begin with **GU** at the 5' splice site and end with **AG** at the 3' splice site, with an internal **branch point** adenine; the intron is excised as a **lariat**. (3) **Polyadenylation:** the 3' end is cleaved and poly(A) polymerase adds a tail of about 200 adenines, which protects the mRNA, aids nuclear export and translation, and influences its lifetime. The mature mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm.

rows: Addition of 7-methylguanosine through a 5'-5' triphosphate bond
Protects from degradation, aids export and translation initiation
Introns removed by the spliceosome (GU...branch point A...AG); exons joined
Cleavage after AAUAAA and addition of about 200 adenines
blocks.caption: Processing of pre-mRNA.

blocks.title: Length of a processed mRNA
blocks.prompt: A pre-mRNA is 15,000 nucleotides long and contains 9 exons that total 2,400 nucleotides. A poly(A) tail of 200 adenines is added. Ignoring the cap, what fraction of the pre-mRNA is removed as introns, and how long is the mature mRNA including its tail?

steps.text: Mature mRNA length including the tail:

blocks.answer: 84% of the pre-mRNA is intron and the mature mRNA is about 2,600 nucleotides including the tail.

blocks.markdown: **Splicing errors and disease.** Splice sites are recognised by their consensus sequences, so a point mutation in the GU or AG of an intron, or the creation of a cryptic splice site, can lead to exon skipping, intron retention or use of a wrong site. For example, some mutations at splice junctions of the beta-globin gene cause beta-thalassaemia by reducing normal splicing and the production of beta-globin chains.

blocks.title: Alternative splicing
blocks.text: Alternative splicing is the production of different mature mRNAs from the same pre-mRNA by including or excluding different exons (or using different splice sites). Different protein isoforms result, so one gene can encode several proteins. A large majority of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced.

blocks.markdown: **Examples and significance.** The *calcitonin/CGRP* gene is spliced differently in the thyroid (producing calcitonin) and in neurons (producing calcitonin gene-related peptide). Immunoglobulin heavy chain pre-mRNA is spliced to give a membrane-bound form on B cells or a secreted form in plasma cells. Tissue-specific splicing regulators (splicing enhancers and silencers, with proteins such as SR proteins) choose between alternatives. This is one reason humans, with about 20,000 protein-coding genes, produce a much larger number of distinct proteins.

blocks.title: Counting isoforms
blocks.prompt: A gene has 3 'cassette' exons, each of which may be independently included or skipped, flanked by constitutive exons. How many different mRNA isoforms can be made?

steps.text: Each cassette exon has two states (in or out).
Check that the answer makes sense: independent inclusion or skipping multiplies, so the count is a power of two.

blocks.answer: 8 isoforms (in practice, regulation means fewer are actually made).

items: RNA polymerase II needs general transcription factors (TFIID binds the TATA box) to form the preinitiation complex.
Elongation 5' to 3' on the template; termination follows the AAUAAA signal.
Pre-mRNA is capped (7-methylguanosine), spliced (spliceosome removes introns) and polyadenylated.
Alternative splicing gives several proteins from one gene.

blocks.title: Clinical link: inhibitors of transcription
blocks.text: Alpha-amanitin from the death-cap mushroom binds and inhibits RNA polymerase II, blocking mRNA synthesis, which is why poisoning mainly damages the liver and other metabolically active tissues. Rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase but not the human enzymes (pharmacology teaching examples).

points: RNA polymerase II, assembled with general transcription factors at the promoter, transcribes protein-coding genes in three stages: initiation, elongation and termination.
Pre-mRNA is capped at the 5' end, spliced by the spliceosome to remove introns, and given a 3' poly(A) tail.
Alternative splicing produces multiple protein isoforms from one gene; splice-site mutations cause disease.

questions.stem: Which structure is added to the 5' end of eukaryotic pre-mRNA?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the cap protects the mRNA and aids translation.
distractorRationale.b: The poly(A) tail is at the 3' end.
distractorRationale.c: A lariat is the excised intron structure.
distractorRationale.d: The TATA box is a DNA promoter element, not part of the RNA.

questions.explanation: A 7-methylguanosine is attached to the 5' end by a 5'-5' triphosphate link. The cap protects against exonuclease degradation and is needed for efficient export and translation.

questions.stem: Which general transcription factor component binds to the TATA box to begin assembly of the RNA polymerase II preinitiation complex?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: TFIID, containing TBP, recognises the TATA box.
distractorRationale.b: DNA ligase works in DNA replication and repair.
distractorRationale.c: Poly(A) polymerase adds the 3' tail after transcription.
distractorRationale.d: The spliceosome removes introns from the transcript.

questions.explanation: TBP, a subunit of TFIID, binds the TATA box and bends the DNA, allowing other general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II to assemble. RNA polymerase II cannot initiate alone.

questions.stem: A patient presents with severe liver injury after eating wild mushrooms. The toxin responsible, alpha-amanitin, inhibits RNA polymerase II. Which step of gene expression is directly blocked?

options.text: Synthesis of pre-mRNA from protein-coding genes

questions.correctOptionText: Synthesis of pre-mRNA from protein-coding genes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: RNA polymerase II transcribes protein-coding genes.
distractorRationale.c: tRNA charging is done by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
distractorRationale.d: Ribosomal RNA is mostly made by RNA polymerase I.

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase II synthesises pre-mRNA for protein-coding genes, so its inhibition stops production of new mRNA and thus protein synthesis. Cells with high metabolic activity, such as hepatocytes, are damaged first.

questions.stem: Which sequence features mark the ends of an intron in pre-mRNA?

options.text: GU at the 5' end and AG at the 3' end
AG at the 5' end and GU at the 3' end
AUG at the 5' end and a stop codon at the 3' end
TATA at the 5' end and poly(A) at the 3' end

questions.correctOptionText: GU at the 5' end and AG at the 3' end

distractorRationale.a: Correct: introns begin with GU and end with AG.
distractorRationale.c: AUG is the start codon and stop codons are not intron borders.
distractorRationale.d: TATA is a promoter element in DNA and poly(A) is a tail added after cleavage.

questions.explanation: The 5' splice site begins with GU and the 3' splice site ends with AG, with a branch point adenine inside the intron. Mutations in these conserved nucleotides disrupt splicing.

questions.stem: In thyroid C cells the calcitonin/CGRP gene yields calcitonin, whereas in neurons the same gene yields calcitonin gene-related peptide. What mechanism explains this?

options.text: Alternative splicing and polyadenylation of the same pre-mRNA in different tissues
Different genes are present in the two cell types
Reverse transcription of mRNA in neurons
Loss of the gene from thyroid cells during development

questions.correctOptionText: Alternative splicing and polyadenylation of the same pre-mRNA in different tissues

distractorRationale.a: Correct: different exon selection yields different mRNAs and proteins.
distractorRationale.b: All somatic cells carry the same genome.
distractorRationale.c: Reverse transcription is not involved in normal tissue-specific expression.
distractorRationale.d: The gene is not lost from thyroid cells.

questions.explanation: A single pre-mRNA can be processed in tissue-specific ways, with different exons joined and different polyadenylation sites used. This produces two different mRNAs and proteins from one gene.

questions.stem: A pre-mRNA of 20,000 nucleotides contains 12 exons with a combined length of 3,000 nucleotides. What percentage of the pre-mRNA is removed as introns? Give your answer in percent (%).
questions.explanation: Intron length equals 20,000 - 3,000 = 17,000 nucleotides. As a fraction of the pre-mRNA, 17,000 / 20,000 = 0.85, so 85% is removed during splicing.

questions.stem: A gene has 5 cassette exons, each of which can independently be included or excluded from the mature mRNA, with all other exons always included. Assuming every combination is possible, how many different mRNA isoforms could be produced? Give a number of isoforms.
questions.explanation: Each cassette exon has two states, included or skipped, and the choices are independent, so the number of combinations is 2^5 = 32. In real cells, regulation restricts the number of isoforms actually produced.

questions.stem: True or false: The poly(A) tail of an mRNA is encoded by a run of thymines at the end of the gene and is transcribed directly.
questions.explanation: The poly(A) tail is added after transcription: the RNA is cleaved downstream of the AAUAAA signal and poly(A) polymerase adds about 200 adenines without a template.

questions.stem: Describe the three stages of transcription by RNA polymerase II, including the role of the general transcription factors.
markingGuide: Initiation: TFIID (TBP) binds the TATA box; other general factors and RNA polymerase II form the preinitiation complex; TFIIH unwinds DNA and phosphorylates the CTD to release the polymerase.
Elongation: polymerase reads the template 3' to 5' and synthesises RNA 5' to 3'; no primer is needed; the CTD recruits processing factors.
Termination: transcription past the polyadenylation signal AAUAAA, cleavage of the RNA downstream and release of the polymerase.
RNA polymerase II needs general transcription factors and cannot initiate alone.
questions.explanation: Transcription proceeds from assembly at the promoter to RNA synthesis and finally to termination at the polyadenylation signal.

questions.stem: Outline the three main processing steps of pre-mRNA and explain how alternative splicing allows one gene to encode several proteins. Give one consequence of a mutation at a splice site.
markingGuide: 5' capping with 7-methylguanosine: protects from exonucleases, aids export and translation.
Splicing by the spliceosome: introns (GU...A...AG) removed as lariats and exons joined.
Polyadenylation: cleavage after AAUAAA and addition of about 200 adenines; stability and export.
Alternative splicing: inclusion or skipping of exons (or alternative splice sites) gives different mRNAs and protein isoforms; tissue-specific regulators control it.
Splice-site mutation can cause exon skipping, intron retention or cryptic site use, giving a defective protein (e.g. beta-thalassaemia).
questions.explanation: Processing converts pre-mRNA into mature mRNA, and the flexibility of splicing multiplies the proteome; errors at splice sites cause disease.
